!OLD DISSENT ING CHAPELS IN
LANCASHIRE.
By nix REV. B. NIGIErMiALE.
9.--T. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. (Coodihried.)

With the new minister came also a new chapel. The old chapel, as previously stated, was erected in 1710, and according to the Evangelieal Magazine" for 1820 Fits norin a dilapidated state at the time of Mr. Vials settlement. But When the people chose a new minister, they resolved also to have a new chapel, and for this purpose subscribed among themselves .El,BOO. The old structure was then taken down, and a building of a modern construc- tion commenced, which is not yet completed.- It was, perhaps, titling, at any rate it is suggestive, that with the old man who hail served the church for nearly half a century, should pass away the building which had become hoary with age. The new chapel was opened for worship on Thursday, December 711,. 1820, the Rev. Dr. Raffles, of Liver- pool, peached rim 2 (or. i., Id 111, and the Ile, James Parsons, of York. from Isaiah iv., 9. The origin of the Sunday School has already been noticed. For thirty years the scholars and teachers utilized the aiz&s, vestry, and pews of the chapel for this purpose, but in 1537 a school was built. The upper room served for the girls and week- night services, •ml the lower for boys. Mr. Vint resigned in 1840 "in consequence of the failure of his health." His death took place in January, 1842. His successor was the
REV, JOHN EDMONDS.

..... He was a native of Poole, in Dorsetshire, being born there in 1795. Having been accepted by the Lon- don Missionary Society. he was sent to Gosport to be I educated under Dr. Rogue. In 182 L along with his wife, he embarked for Calciitta, and went to strengthen the mission at Chinsuriiii, close by. bail- ing health, necessitated Ids return to England in , 1827. His tirst charge at home was Hope Chapel, Shelton, in Staffonlshire, commencing his labours there in May. 1828. In May, 1841, be removed to St. Helens. Whilst here the Jubilee of the Sunday school, was celebrated in 1854 i. "it is reCOrtiefi of him," says Mr. Ward, "and well remembered by many, that the missionary spirit, which in his early life had impelled him to go to India, never left him, and he exhibited it, among other ways, in devoting his annual vaeation to deputation engagements for the London Missionary Society," and the obituary notice of him in "Tine Congregational Year Book," for 1859 further states : -" There is scarely part of the three kingdoms that he did not visit to plead ita claims. Everywhere he was a welcome visitor. Next to the spiritual welfare of his tiock,the salvation of the perishing heathen was the object for which he lived, and in sympathy with which he died." Mr. Edmond:, died suddetily on Sunday. March hot, 18.18. In the morning he had preached trom Eph. iii., 12., and in the evening his congrega- tion was shocked with the announcement that the devoted pastor was no more. In the St. Helens Chapel is a handsome marble tablet erected to his memory a copy of the inscription upon which is into subjoined :—" Sacred to the memory of the Rev. John Edmonds (interred in the vault beneath), I formerly a missionary in India, and afterwards I successively Pastor of the Church assembling in ! Hop: Chapel, Shelton, and of that worshipping within the.se walls. Ile exerriseol his ministry with much affection and fidelity for lit years, and fell asleep in J esus on Sunday evening, March 21:4,1858, aged 59 years. Also of John George, eldest son of tine above who died on the 18th ofJune,lB2d, aged 31 years. Christ is all, and in all." Mr. Edmonds was succeeded at St. Helens by the

He was tglucated at ttancaslure College, and entered the ministry in 1880, coming in that soar to St. Helens. " His brief but memorable ministry M St. Helens,' says Mr. Word, " was brought to a o low in 1887, by h removal to the newly formed church at Chorhomroad. Manchester." At tins place the doctor still labours, and during lois ministry there has been built up one of the strongest and 'nest enterprising churches in Lancashire. It is in every sense a model clutrelt, and it is not too touch to wy that' the eyes of all (the Lancashire churches) wait upon it" for guidance and Mit. Upon the doctor himself the highest honours have been heaped of which the denomination has command. In 1879 loe occupied the chair of the Lancashire Congregational tnion when the meetings were held at Bolton and three .-earts after he lootitme President of the Ontgregational tnion of England and Wales. Few tnen are no much in rstutwt by the churches for special occasions, and doubtless there are times when the good doctor is made to feel that there are penalties attached to grearmss, and inconveniences to popularity. The present minister,

whilst a student at Airedale College, preached for the first time at St. What. tan the sth of April, 1663. In the following September ha was invited to the pastorate, upon which he entered August 14th, 1864 " his term at !College not basing expired till that time." The re-opening servnees were contoured tan Sunday, April 2701, when the Rev. Samuel Pearson. M.A., of Liverpool, was the preacher ; tan TusslaY, April 2911,. when an organ recital was given by Mr. W. ... , . ..... St. Helens Chapel stamls in a busy thoroughfare, and I it is well situatol hn the religi .. us requirementn of the town. It in a large brick structun, has a mant corn- : mauling appearance anti stands in the centre of a rapa- cious graveyanl. To the right is the school, a really ,rgterrterlili,e, quite collegiate in style. div.head: TWO WOMEN STABBED IN LONDON
div.p: TWO WOMEN STABBED IN LONDON

At an early hour on Tues.lay morning two women pasaing through a courtway in WhitoTasi, St. Luke's, I London, were accosted by an elderly labouring man. On their refusing to go with him he stabbed them both, but not severely. A policeman followed, and captured him, but not without a desperate struggle, in which the man attempted to stab the officer. There was much excite- ment in the district, a "Jock the Ripper" scare being raised directly.

ATTEMITED AIURDER AND SUICIDE AT WIDNES. A MISERABLE TALE.

• At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. IL l'ilkington and Mr. ii. Wide Deacon, Catherine Doyle, aged 37, wife of Patrick Doyle, , , chemical labourer, I, Sutton's-lane, Widnes, was charged with having, on Thurslay, attempted to commit suicide and also at the same thne to murder lies O blind child, aged three years, by drowning it—Peter ! Dennett, a labourer, said on Tim-slay morning at 11 oo'clock, he was working near ifittownl., when Ike saw the prisoner coning idong. She appeared to be very "strange" and he watched her. Site went to the edge of a pit, sat down Otto" rock' of stones with the child in her arms, and a few 111111LIIIS afteniards he mimed her. De went to the pit and SAW the woman just crawling out. She appeared to be very miserable and said she would make away with herselL—The prisoner solid she did not know what she woo doing. Site did noit mean to harm the child. She had intend.' taking the child to its father and then doing what site liked to herself—Tl,' husband came forward and said his wife wat always drunk and Ile could dote, good with her. On Monday site was drunk when he came home, and she had to get upstairs on her hands and kno:s. On Tuesday morning she was outside waiting for the pulolic-houses too open. Site had been just the same for the last sis or seven years. He had bison separatosi from her, and had allowed her 12s. 6)1. a wash, but sht• had lived with hitn the past two years. She had even spent in drink the money Ike had given her to take the child to the Eye infinnary at Liverpool, and she Intl " drunk money " given to her by Mr. Deacem for the same purpose.—Mr. Pilkington Will you undertake to look after her if we let her go.—Doyle: I cannot look after her and mind my work.—Mr. Pilkington (to the prisoner) : Will you behave yourself if we let you ~it.—The prisoner If he will allow me so much I will take the children and look after them.—Doyle : You must not take the children I will take the 'children myself. Mr. Pilkington said the magistrates would give the woman another cisme° and allow her too go this time. If ',nought up again she would I be severely dealt with.—Doyle whimt the magistrates to, grant a separation, he to have the children, ant! Mr. Pilkingtoin said they must settle that betwom them- , I selves.

The Vienna correspondent of the `. Drily Telegraph " says :--A trial involving einomustances of an exception- ally romantie character will no to ton, the tribunal oot Ragusa, nest month. Allout twenty years ago a sant of the ncighbourho sad of Raguri, being no longer able to support Ids wife, emigratril to tie: United States. leaving his better half in large of the village larks: From the first luck smiled on in,,, oral to. was able to send the priest fifty flo orins a month for ilk wife. As his position improved he increanal the amount .1 his remit- tances, but the priest only handed five florins a month to the woman. This went on for fifteen yearn, when the priest forged a certitivate of the husband's death and placed it in the hands of his wife, whose death he like- wise certified in a hinged document and sent it to the husband in America. Afterwanls he piously betoaok himself to Oulu. The husband visited Paris, Vienna. Trieste, and finally Ragusa. On landing at the harbour a beggar woman accosted him and asked him for AIMa. They recognised each other simultansrinly. The beggar was Ids wife, whom he believed to have been dead sev- eral years. The priest has been arrested, and will be tried. In all pr. rbability a second marriage contracted in the meantbne by the husband with a rieh American lady will IN allUlakd.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 7, 1839.

Mr- The Liberal Unionists were in full Ch'"be-cluin force at Birmingham, on Monday Again. evening, when they met in the Town Hull as 'the Grand Committee of the Bir- mingham Liberal Unionist Association." To say that they were in full force does not mean that the hall was full far from it, but there was a full muster—for Lilmral Unionists. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN !IIIVERIBIl; there is a Grand Committee, and it is now a matter of worse that he should be the grand chairman. There was a thee when he would have scorned the itre of the word "grand.' That was the really grand time when he had the people at his back. But now those days are over; he has lost the substance, and so be rushes after the shadow; he is chairman of a Grand Committee, auid he moves in the narrow circle of grandees. tie had a good deal to sac on Monday, and he sought, as hiss been usual with him of late, to make it out that he is still a Liberal of Liberals, although his days and nights have been given to the support of a Tory Government. He has one piece of news—news unlmown to anybody but the member for West Birmingham—and that is that " the tactics of the old Parliamentary hand have completely broken down: But Joseph must have had a dream; them are certainly visions about when he puts forth such a statement as this; for it is altogether at variance with the revelations of the bye-elee- tions,which conclusively indicate that the old Par- liamentary hand has the Hoeing tide with Inm. A. grand chairman of a Grand Committee toes things.. perhaps, from an altogether different point of view. For instance, in the day, that are no more, Mr. JOHEYIi CHAMBERLAIN, who was then the rising hope of the Radical party, emphasised one opini in by saying—" I hate coercion; 1 hate the name hate the thing" Now what Radicals still ,all coercion is emphatically referred to by the member for West Birmingham to'' the jusL and impar- tial enforcement of th, law." He has changed his point of view ; lict what of th, thing itrelf Has that changed If coerchm was hateful, : , four years ago, go all honest Liberals, has it ceased to be haleful Has coercion ceased to be coercion bee :use Mr. Cr AMBIKRI,V, has ceased to be a leader of the Libm 41 party These are questions which have again and amino been put to the autocran, of the Graral Committee of. the Birmingham Liberal Unionist Asseciation ; but as yet be has ...et found it movenient to Ansa, them.

Turning to 31.. Ctismumut.iss's prow ammo —it is not of 1:0111.81A 'Ale Radical rogramme which he , once dinned in 4 sir ears-- -we bad that, titer all his !elaborate phut... for the puaihase of the land of Ireland, he is,content to popose to the Govern- ment that, ‘. insteul of introducim, a bill upon which they waist stake their existsnce, and by which they must stand m fall, they should submit their proNsals to Parliai sent in the shape :if rms.,- lotions, and invite upon them a fine and a frank discuasiisi, inn' a full eiticism from all quarters of the Imam" The fa A of the matter is Mr. CIWILMRLA IS knows perfectly well that he cannot claim the support either of Um Government or of Lord HARSINOTOS to the latest of the many seta:sues he has mopounded s.d he is anxious that his failure should be hidden in a dotal of words. He is :MA as shifty and unsound on the question .of local government for Ireland. Nobody knows better than ho that any further power which is put in th 3 hands 14 the Nationa- lists will be used—and rightly used—as it lever for obtaining Millie Rule. And how does he propose to meet this difficulty He says : If there exists in some minds a notion that these great privileges would be wrongly or illegally abused, I think that might be met by provisions that in such a case appeal should be had to a high judicial tribunal, and that if any local authority refused to obey the decrees of such a court, it should be declared to be in contempt, and thereupon its powers should pass as a manor of course to other hands.
This is comical—roally comical, trot:mil is to havo

" Vaulting ambition doesn't " o'erleap itself" it Winwitit-with-Hulme it doesn't leap at all. There isa vacancy for thetownship on the Warring- ton Board t.l Guardians MA nobody seems willing , to till the gap : and NS a flatter of fact the town- ship is nurelresentc4l. Happy township! which has flung away ambition--the sin by which the I angels fell.

Viscount Hinton gets his living anal shames his aristocratic relations by playing A piano-organ. But he leis been overdoing his part : and,for refus- ing to 1110V0 On " when requested, he was fined Ills., on Monday, at the Marlborough-st. Police Court. Organ-grinders mist obey the law even when they are Viscounts. Hinton must see to it in future that he does not work too hard when he is playing.

John Foster, collier of St. Helens, was collared whilst night poaching at Rainford on the :Nth Aug. :Ile called on his mates, who made off, to oilcan hack and' mill " the keepers lint his mates preferred running to milling, and have not bowmen since. Foster seems to have been an old "night hand f. but his little game is stopped. He in shut MI for six weeks at least from the " delights of a shiny night in the season of the year.

The sudden death from sunstroke of Mr. Firth, M.P., is a serious loss to the London County Council. He was in the prime of life—forty- seven toily--stud looked younger. He fought the battle if kcal government for the Metropolis in splendid style, and there was every prospect, if he had lived, of his doing good work as the right arm of the Council. He was a Torkshirenian and is Quaker—a Quaker with the fighting spirit in him.

All hail to the Victors The election of Runcorn Commissioners ended as the tnajority of people expected, in the return of the tire retiring members, and they will be heartily welcomed by their col- leagues at the first meeting. Although defeated, Mr. larwood is not disheartened, and he intends yet once again to attempt to secure the seat he so ardently covets. After the declaration of the poll, Mr. Abel disappeared from view, and his future intentiottS can only be guessed. Formerly the Runcorn Commissioners were fond , of speech-making over the town's business, and I seldom did the meeting conclude under an hour and a half. At the last meeting the Committees pro- ceedings were all moved, seconded, and carried. in ! the short space of five minutes and the previous month the meeting terminated in nine minutes. !Stich expedition is almost enou4/1 to dumbfound 1 the entire population, and it srems as though Mr. I Abel were not needed.

In conformity with the custom ! of the past few years the Market Hall was con- verted into the place of polling, the returning officer's booth being a shop at the top entrance, 1 while the Candidates 41 also their offices inside the building. ALLEGRO FIGHT AT BRIDOE•FOOT. Edward Carroll and Catherine Carroll. husband mid wife, and John and Edward Carroll, their Punt, answered summonsee at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday. charging them with having assaulted Edward Craddock, a tallow dealer, on the previous Friday. Craddock was charged on a cram- summons with having assaulted the four Carrolls. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for Craddock, told the magistrates that his client had stables in a yard at Bridge-foot, in which yard was also located a caravan in which the CarrolTs live. On Friday morning Craddock, he said, was passing the van, when something was said shout a horse belonging to him. The elder Carroll, it was alleged, knocked Craddock down, and then, lifting. him up, threw him over hie head. Craddock recmved a wound on, the head, and was going away to have it dressed, when Mrs. Carroll came out of the van and hit him on the head with an iron bar. The sons then came up, and also assaulted him. Mr. P. navies, who was for the Carmlls, contended that all the parties were equally to blame, and that Craddock and the elder Carroll had a tight, in which the former got the worst of it. The magistrates bound the elder Carroll and Craddock over in personal recognisances, each side to pay their own costa. A MUTMI.EI.- RAILWAY TnArathmin. A labouring man named John Doyle Was brought before the Warrington magistrates ou Monday, on charge of havingjourneyed from Preston to Warring- ton on the London and North-Western Railway, on Saturday night, without having paid bin fare, with intent to cheat the company. It appeared from the evidence of a railway detective that on the arrival' at Bank Quay Station of the limited mail on Sat ur- day night prisoner was seen to alight from a third class carriage. When asked for his ticket he admitted that he had not got one, and as he would give no aatisfactnry account of how he Came to be at Warrington he was given into custody. Ile told the officials that he had travelled by an earlier train from Lancaster to l'reston, and that he had no money, hot when his pocke:s were searched be was found to have two shillings and a penny in his pocket. Prisoner gave the magistrates to understand that his origi- nal intention was to travel from Lancaster to Pres- ton, and no further, but he got some drink at the former place. Ile ala took some with him when he entered a train at Lancaster and in consequence got into a " muddied" condition. Ile alighted at Preston, and got into another train, under the impression that he had not reached his destination, but had to change trains. The Mayor intimated that the magistrates were of opinion that there was a doubt as to the fraudulent intention of the pri- soner. He would have to pay the lock-up fee, 25., and:would also be ordered to pay the railway fare, 2s. ltd., due to the company. Ile agreed to do that. but as the railway officials doubted the correctness of an address he gave, it was questionable whether they would succeed in recovering the amount.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND LIBERAL UNIONIST POLICY.

Mr. Chamberlain, arliln,sing, the Liberal Unionist Grand Coininittee at Birmingham, lln Monday night, reviewed the politieal aro:die:l, Ue asirert.l that the adininistration of Ireland by the present Government had been a signal SCI,-and that both at home and abroad the honour anti the intensts of the country had been maintained. The Government of the Unionist alliance was stranger fl than whenfOrtlllat three years : ago, while the Oppusition was divided in leadership and distract.] in slimed. He asked moderate Gladstonians hOW long they were going to altos. the Jacobins to lead them, and if they would refuse support to the Unionist policy of endeavouring to deal with the most pressing Irish grievances nmarding the land, local government, and university edurntion. Respecting the land, he advised the 'Ministry to submit resolutions to the Commons before bringing in a Bill, do to loimi govern- ment, lie recommended precautions against its abuse ; and respecting university education. he remarked that, seeing the English and Scotch would not give up denominational endowments for inlucation, :Ire policy of equality demanded such endowment in Ireland. He repeated his objections to a Hume Rule Parliament as destructive to the interests of the I7nited Kingdom, and likely to lead to the risk of civil war.

div.p: BURNLEY GAZETTE, February 23rd. 7IIE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeahle one. Apart front the terrible
iisks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion,

with all its thrilling scenes, tlie collier has to pursue his work at times tuekt circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford load, Burnley, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how ho let ropeatoilly hail to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water am, cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such condition idi employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had ti miounier them in other mining hi romiegrienee. Ile first commenced with pains in hi, 1., ...,I.Vtlllllgradually extended to other parts of the body.• low,- said Mr. Knowles, "that I was obliged to be coverel- with blankets and have a chair day. It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak t' had to have the help of a stick to get across the door. I was terribly troubled with O. - turn, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of : in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for bows and got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. . seemed to make me worse, and I got so that my friends g.ave me up and the doctor ventured to offer no hope of a cure. At last I read one of Warner's pamphlets, sent for 'a bottle of 'Warner's SAFF Core,' and oh ! how much good it did me. In a few weeks I was o new man. My appetite lot-aimed, the weakness disappeared, and 1 - . went back to my work n,lhig stronger than I had done for vats."

THE GAS QUESTION.

- - Sir,—! hope all gait consumers will read with the greatest of care the statement by Mr. Alderman Davies on the gas question. He states that the sum saved to the consumers is £20,917 19s. but he Is to state where this amount is, or its value. Against tlAs I estimate that for the past three or four years the gas consumer:olmm been paying from 25 per cent., and upwards more for gas than i value, taking into account the mice at which it is sold at other towns. Take, for instance, Ilalifax gas is supplied at Is. 9d. per thousand, and at Widnes, the price, 1. think, is under 2s. If anyone wislim to estimate the value of the gas supplied by the Committee let him examine the gas fittings in Bold-street Chapel. Though the fittings were new a short time since, they are beday in shad condition became of the impuritim having destmyed them : and Stir Trustees will hove to clean the ceiling mein, or all the light will be tot. div.head: TRE HOURS OF LABOUR QUESTION.
div.p: TRE HOURS OF LABOUR QUESTION.

.... Sir,—There is a cam reported in last week's " Examiner" which deserves some attention from the working-men of Warrington in particular. It is that of one of the draymen of Mum,. 6reenall, Whitler, and Co., who was fined at Daresbury Petty Semions for hat. ing been asleep whilst in charge of kin horses and dray on the highway. The man appears to have said as an excuse that he supposed he couldn't help going to sleep because ho had been at work no long, and what sin yon think he said were his hours on that particular day? Simply these he began at half-pas, live in the morning, and finiolool at a quarter to eleven at night. That is to say, out of the t malty-four 11.1UrS, he was, if his statement be true, at work seventeen and a quarter, and had the remaining six and titree quarters for sleep. recreation, and selbimproyement. Ido not know whether this is an average or an exceptional day's work for a Wilder- spool drayman, but it is worth noticing. As the law at present stands--and I hope it will he altered before long in the direction of a eompulmry shortening of the hours labour—Mesors Oreenall, Whitley and Co. have a perfect right to fix the hours of labour of their work' people at any limit they choose. That is a matter between them and their workpeople. Hut in this case it must not he forgotten that the principal partner in this firm is member of Parliament for Warrington—the representative of an e...sentbdly working-class constitu- ency,' and if there is one rause worth fighting for and ! safe-guarding by working people it is the cause of reasonable hours of labour. I consider that a working- man who votes for or supports in ant way a candidate, Pa' he Liberal or Tory, who knowingly practices or coun- tenances " sweating " in any of its odious forms, plays traitor to the best interests of the class to which he Imlongs.—Yours truly, A WAGE-EARNER. Warringtun, Sept., 1889.

div.head: orli NATIONAL POVERTY.—THE DOCK LABOURERS.
div.p: orli NATIONAL POVERTY.—THE DOCK LABOURERS.

Sir,—At the present time the antagonists are engned in fierce scar—which will conquer in undecided. If popular sympathy is a factor in the battle, the issue is certain. The state of conflict at present is—wealth and! dogged determination on one side poverty and popular! sympathy on the other. It is a contest between might , and right. Dean Oakley in last Saturday's "Manchester Guanlian " gives his readers a thrilling account, front his , personal experience. as to how these dock labourers exist : —the hunger, cold and privation that they endure; the ; hundreds that flock around the dock gates in the early morning breakfastless and hungry. Many of them have, had the stones of the street for their bed ; an archway or I a dnorway, or an entry for shelter, turned out of the I common fodging-house at eleven o'clork at night, not ! having the means to pay for such a bed as the common I lodging-house affords. They have then the run of the ! streets, and to keep clear of the policeman mon] six o'clock in the morning. Then they have to fight for a I chance to earn sd. sometimes 40. a hour, for, it may 1,. I two hours—when they receive the magnificent sum of I 10d., and are told there will be no M. work that day. ; Often times men who have walked Oxot all night, fail to get ant work at all the next day, and a day of fasting j sum:en:hid by a night of trainping ensues. Thew oar the I conditions of life of tholsands of what are called casual I labourers in the East of London. Are they not in the right to try and better their conditions Sixpence an hour is not a great wage for the labori- ous work they have to do,especially when the work is not continent', and the man is liable to be discharged, or' what is Palled "granted." at any minute. Thousands of these men rarely make 10, a week. Who will blame Gran for inking? Who will oat wish that they may succeed in their reasonable demands ? lam glad to s'e that they have friends and sympathisers in all parts of the country, and that they are sustained and cheered by such men an Dean Oakley and Cardinal Manning. It never can low that the conditions of trade at the ilocks of the largest and richest port in the world are no had that they cannot afford casual laboureni 8.1, an hour, and that thousands at men who handle the rich merchandise of the port of I,..ndim should exist in a state of destitu- tion and semi-starvation. It would he incredible but that we have no many reliable witnessesdaily testifying to the fact, year after year. Let us hope that this terrible strike ma'Y end by twittering the conditions of life of the dock NG-Wirers and other kindred employments in mod- ern Babylon. In contrast with the foregoing, I notice that 28 Dural families. with 518 relatives filling 1,013 officeo, root the country £9.260.090. 33 families of Maniiikeo with 1328 nlatiies tilling 1.252 offices coat £8,305.950. 200 familieo ii Eirls with 3.391 relatives, filling 5.90 offices. coat the country £30.115,182. giving' a total £48,181. 202. Look on this picture and on that, and draw your own ennelesions. The contrast is appalling. —I am, Sir. yours respectfully, CV MOO. Sankey Bridges, Sept. 6th, 1889.

div.head: TIIE WORKS OF COTNT TOLSTOI.
div.p: TIIE WORKS OF COTNT TOLSTOI.

Sir,—Allow me to thank you most heartily for your able and interesting article on one of the works of this distinguished writer. I wag very pleased, to, to see the extract you gave ftwat this look " What to do." I refer to the story of the per washerwootnan. To me Tol-tooi is one oof the most imposing figures of the present century, and the perusal of lois works has afforded snot the highest pleasure, and given ine a grander conception of humanity and religion than I ever posseused before. I holieve it is a fact that, at the present day, questions' relating to sociology and religion are more rife, and pressing more for intelligoont settlement ,than twer bef..re. , Everyone admits the necessity of sweeping reforms in the social life of the people. Misery and vice in their I direst forms are to be seen around UA overy hand. , Notwithstanding all our enlightment and pr ogntss, and ' tonloaralleled wealth as a nation, tile fact remains, as I true toulay as in the days of JOS., that the poor are I always with at. Indeed, many leaders of thought are of opinion that the poverty and misery of the people are greater now than ever before. I have before me the works of one writer who says tliat the millions of wretched humanity ate daily increasing, and if condition is beaming inevitably more miserable." Another writer says that in spiteof all that has loern done in recent years to better the condition of the people, ill the lower ranks of society a seething maw, of misery, destittition, and vice, has been left untouched by the philanthropist, the social reformer, and the legislator. "it seems," says Mr. Ritchie, " a strange parody upon the present boasted progrow and greatnooss of Britain that over one million of her people should he paupers, and hundreds of thousands of able and willing workers should be denied the opportunity of earning a livelihood." I believe there are many ardent, high-sottled men and women desirous of remedying such a deplorable state of Ithingsand, with many such, the omestions involuntarily- ' arise, " Wltat shall we do?" anti " flow shall we du it f" To all such I would earnestly commend the reading of Misters life and works. They will find there the most exalted ideals of earnest, practical, humane combintsl with the noblest conceptions of a self-sacrifie- ing Christian life. When I had begun to lose faith in I Christianity, and to look upon prodeusing Christians with , somewhat 'distrustful eyes, I WWI brought back to a vivid I senee of thenobility anti grandeur and supreme humanity of the teaching of the Great Master by reading Tolstoi. Tolstoi, like Jesus of Nazareth, went about teaching and doles, good. Of high rank and prat social position, he I renounced all to walk in the footsteps of cone who '• for I our saluw became poor." "He learned the true meaning of life from a simple soldier, and thereby realized that safety for the future is to be obtained onlv be bringing life to the standard of rude sunplicity—adoptosl by tlte common people,by recognising in act,as well as in theory, the brotherhood of man." This principle of life has been rettoymiosl by ('anon. Farrar who asks for anew set of preachers, mot who , ' shall remain single, and who shall live amongst the poor, as poor as they, and whose who ole lives shall pour silent I I contempt upon gold—men infinitely mono noble than the present race of preachers, atol who shall be an exalted , example to all men who make a great feeding trough of , the world, and who live in an atmosphere of senstornefis , .4 self-gratification. But Tolstoi not only preaehes this,he prectierg it. Would that we had many more such ; preachers and doers! I At the present titn?, a considerable anti an increasing nuntbor of intelligent people fond themselves more or lem I dissatisfied with the religious creeds and theological deb- , nitions with which they are familiar ; and there are I many earnest and thoughtful Christian people who are ; ill at twse with some of the popular religious dogmas. ' This is, no doutot, a rebound front the over-dogmatic tendency of past generations, and is a protest ag,ainst unreasonableness and error and the unwarrantable i assumption of authority over tile consciences and minds om f en, and in favour of the great right and duty of. private judgment. Orthodoxy, too often, donanols the surrender of reason. Tolstoi, like Seneca, and Milt., and Rutter. claims to he guided by reason. Ile says. ' "reason, which illuminates our life and impels UA to modify our actions, is not an illusion, and its authority can never he tlenied. To obey reason in the pursuit of , good is the sutotance of the teachings of all the masters of humanity, and it is the substance of the dxtrines of Jesus ; it is reason itself, anti we cannot deny reason by the Use of reason." fie believes, indeed, that religion, ; riehtly undertows], cannot possibly otonflict witlt the test human estimate of justice and pure morality, nor with sound reason. . . . .
